label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Peter, your nine years in payroll deserve to be taken seriously, and I agree with more of your diagnosis than this reply might initially suggest. An informal scheme with no ceiling, no consistent approval route and people negotiating in HR’s office is difficult to defend. Rolling advances can keep somebody permanently behind, leavers do create a recovery risk, and Finance is entitled to demand predictable cash requirements.

Where I part company with you is on “close the window… and then people adjust”. We tried almost exactly the approach you recommend in 2025, and some people adjusted by taking on much worse debt. We eventually reopened the scheme.

For context, we have about 340 staff across Embakasi and Changamwe in Mombasa, mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. We closed advances in February 2025 after Finance pushed back. Their argument was very close to yours, almost word for word in places. We did not simply stop overnight: we gave two months’ notice, directed staff towards the SACCO and held a financial-literacy session with the SACCO.

In the six months after closure, debt-collector and loan-app calls to the office went from a handful to **61 calls logged by reception**. Some apps were calling supervisors whom borrowers had listed as “referees”. At that point, it is no longer entirely the employee’s private contract. Reception is spending time on it, supervisors are being contacted about a subordinate’s debt, and HR is drawn back into the problem without having any useful lever to resolve it.

We also saw unplanned absence rise on the two days after month-end. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers being away “sorting out” loans. I would not claim that every call or absence was caused by the closure; we did not run a controlled study. But the operational pattern was clear enough that we could not dismiss it.

One case stayed with me. A loader at Changamwe came to me when he was already juggling six loan apps, borrowing from one to pay another. It took us four months, working with payroll, to unwind his position. That is considerably more disruptive than processing a rule-based advance through a portal.

The SACCO remains important, but it is not a substitute for every short-term need. Our SACCO loans take two to three weeks to process and require guarantors. That may be suitable for planned borrowing; it is not much help when a child has been sent home over school fees on a Tuesday. Financial literacy is also worth doing, but it has limits. Where somebody earns around KES 28,000 a month, better budgeting does not automatically create enough spare cash to absorb every emergency.

We reopened in September 2025, but not by returning to the informal arrangement. We put it in writing:

- **Maximum 40% of net pay.**
- **Once per pay cycle.**
- **Repaid in full at the next payroll**, with no rollover into another advance.
- **No fee or interest.**
- Requests made through the **payroll portal**, not by coming to negotiate in my office.
- Payroll checks the deductions before approving. The Employment Act limits total deductions to two-thirds of wages, so that check is part of the process. The design ensures that nobody receives an advance and then ends up with nothing at month-end.

Since reopening, we have generally had **55–70 requests a month**, averaging around **KES 9,000 each**. At that average, roughly KES 495,000–630,000 moves through the scheme in a month. Those are requests, incidentally, not necessarily 55–70 different employees, so repeat use is something we monitor separately.

Recovery has been 100% apart from balances on two leavers. The total written off was roughly **KES 14,000 for the year**. That does not make your leaver risk imaginary, Peter — our two cases demonstrate it — but it does mean the risk can be measured and controlled rather than assumed to be unlimited.

Our Finance Manager now defends the scheme himself. The decisive point for him was not a sentimental argument about staff welfare. It was that the forecast impact is bounded and visible. There is a fixed ceiling, a defined request route and a known repayment date. It is no longer a series of surprises appearing during the month.

Nor would I present our experience as proof that an advance scheme is cost-free. Administration takes time, repeat borrowing needs attention, and we did write off money. But those costs are easy to see because they sit in payroll. The costs of absence, missed runs, reception handling collection calls, supervisors being contacted and HR helping somebody untangle six apps are scattered across departments. They do not disappear merely because Finance cannot put them on the advance ledger. I have not converted all of ours into a neat return-on-investment figure, and I would be wary of anyone who did without solid data. I am saying both sides need to be costed.

**Brenda**, for your meeting on the 18th, I would not argue for preserving your current informal arrangement unchanged. I think you can concede that part and still make a strong case against complete closure. You are proposing to replace an unmanaged practice with a controlled policy, not asking Finance to endorse unlimited employee borrowing.

The shape I would put on the table is:

1. **A hard cap.** Our 40% of net pay has worked for us, although your Finance Manager may want to model a lower starting figure. The important thing is that the cap applies without quiet exceptions.
2. **One advance per pay cycle.** No second top-up and no rolling balances.
3. **Full recovery at the next payroll.** Payroll checks the proposed recovery alongside statutory and other deductions, including the two-thirds legal limit and the employee’s remaining pay.
4. **A non-discretionary approval route.** A portal or standard form goes to Payroll, which approves against the rules. Supervisors should not decide whose story is deserving, and HR should not be carrying cash requests around the business.
5. **No interest or administration fee.** This keeps it clearly an advance of salary, not a company loan product.
6. **Rules for repeat users and leavers.** Repeated requests should trigger confidential budgeting or debt support, not a bigger advance. Agree with Payroll how notice periods, final dues and outstanding balances will be handled.
7. **A review period.** Pilot it for six months and give Finance a monthly schedule of request volumes, values, total exposure, repeat usage, recoveries and write-offs.

Finance can then show you the maximum permitted cash impact under the cap, rather than dealing only with anecdotal requests. You can also report actual utilisation against that ceiling.

Before the meeting, I would extract whatever you already have for the last six or twelve months: number and value of advances, how many employees request repeatedly, outstanding leaver balances, and an honest estimate of payroll and HR processing time. On the operational side, look at absence immediately after month-end and any disruptions supervisors can reasonably connect to staff dealing with debt. Your figures may look different from ours, and my 61 calls should not be presented as a prediction for your company. They are evidence that the supposedly external consequences can be logged and measured.

If Finance still prefers closure, ask what baseline and review measures will be used. “People will adjust” should be treated as a testable proposition, not the end of the analysis. Agree to review collection calls, post-payroll absence, supervisor time and any production disruption after three and six months, alongside the expected payroll savings.

Peter, I would now use most of your objections as design requirements: no dependency on rolling credit, no HR discretion, no hidden cash exposure and no casual treatment of leaver balances. My disagreement is with closure as the default remedy. In our case, closing the window did not remove the underlying need; it moved the borrowing somewhere more expensive and brought some of the consequences back through reception, supervisors and operations. A bounded, written scheme has been much easier for us to manage — and, importantly, much easier for Finance to forecast.
